sections.html:
Manassas is a small independent city in Northern Virginia and the county seat of Prince William County. It is its own government, separate from the county, and it borders the independent city of Manassas Park. The city covers 9.9 square miles. The 2020 census counted 42,772 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 44,332.

Because Manassas is an independent city, the county does not assess your house or bill you for it. The city's Commissioner of the Revenue and Treasurer handle both jobs, so a seller deals with one set of city offices.

Manassas has an older core and a large amount of housing from the 1980s. About 35 percent of the city's housing stock went up between 1980 and 1989, the city's biggest period of growth. A house from that decade is now around 40 years old, so roofs, heating and cooling equipment and water heaters may be near the end of their life.

A buyer who needs a mortgage will send an inspector, and the inspector will list those items. A buyer paying cash usually prices them in and moves on. Homeowner vacancy in 2020 was just 0.7 percent, which tells you few houses sit empty for long, but a dated one can still take months to sell the traditional way.

Manassas is served by Virginia Routes 28, 234 and 234 Business. I-66 and US 29 serve the area without passing through the city. The Manassas station is shared by Virginia Railway Express and Amtrak, and it also houses the city's visitor center.

  • VRE commuter trains run through the station.
  • Amtrak's Cardinal, Northeast Regional and Crescent stop at Manassas.

The mean commute is about 34.7 minutes, longer than the Virginia figure of 28.2. About 73 percent of workers drive alone and 4 percent take transit. If your house is close to the station or a main route, say so when you talk to a buyer.

Real estate tax in Manassas is paid in two installments, and the fiscal year begins July 1. The Commissioner of the Revenue assesses all real property. The Treasurer collects the money.

PaymentDue dateOffice
First installmentDecember 5Treasurer
Second installmentJune 5Treasurer
Assessment of real propertyFiscal year begins July 1Commissioner of the Revenue

The Treasurer's Real Estate Tax page has the details. Questions about collection go to 703-257-8241, and City Hall is at 9027 Center Street.

If your lender collects taxes through escrow, your mortgage company probably pays the bill. The Treasurer's office does not send copies to homeowners, so if a bill reaches you, pass it on to the lender.

This matters when you sell. Before a closing date is set, find out whether the current installment is paid, who paid it, and how the settlement agent will split the year between you and the buyer. Ask for that line on the settlement statement.

Residents aged 65 or older and certain disabled people may qualify for exemption or deferral through Tax Relief. Call the Treasurer to ask whether you qualify.

Delinquent accounts may be handed to a collection firm. Under Virginia law, not getting a bill does not erase penalty and interest, so an unpaid balance keeps growing even if the mail never arrived. If you owe back taxes, the balance is usually paid out of the sale proceeds at closing, and a payoff figure from the Treasurer tells you the exact amount.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works, step by step
sections.html:
A cash sale uses the same Virginia process as any sale, except nobody lends money. No appraisal holds things up, and a buyer's inspector does not hand you a repair list.

  • Gather the deed, your recent tax bills and any payoff letters for loans or liens.
  • Tell the buyer about the condition of the house and when you need to close.
  • Pick a settlement company to search title and prepare the paperwork.
  • Agree on a closing date and sign.

You choose the timing, and you hand over the house as it stands. Nothing has to be cleaned out or fixed first.

sections.h2: Closing costs on the seller's side
sections.html:
The main state charge on the seller is the grantor tax: 50 cents for each $500 of value. Sellers carry it by default, though a contract can shift it to the buyer. Before the clerk will record your deed, the first page has to show the price.

Your settlement agent works out the final figures, so ask for a written estimate early. If you wonder whether a city rule applies to your lot, a call to City Hall settles it before you sign.

sections.h2: What to bring when you start
sections.html:
A short folder saves days. Pull together the deed if you have it, the last two tax bills, any mortgage or lien payoff letters, and a note on who lives in the house. If the house is rented, add the lease. If heirs share ownership, list every name and where each person lives.

Then walk the house with fresh eyes. Note the age of the roof, the furnace or heat pump and the water heater, because those are the items a buyer will ask about first. You do not need to repair anything. The notes just help you get a straight number from the buyer.

sections.h2: What happens between offer and closing
sections.html:
After you accept an offer, the settlement company searches title and looks for liens, unpaid taxes and anything else that could block the deed. If the search turns up a back tax balance, it is paid from your proceeds. You sign the deed, the company records it, and you receive your funds. With no mortgage underwriter involved, the date on the contract is usually the date you close.

A seller who lives out of state can often sign through the settlement company without traveling. Tell the buyer about that early so the paperwork is set up for it.

The same few situations come up again and again.

  • Aging 1980s systems that need replacing.
  • Rental houses with tenants or deferred repairs.
  • Inherited houses with heirs in other states.
  • Escrow and tax paperwork that has to be settled at closing.

A direct sale lets you set the date and walk away without a punch list.

faqs.q: Is Manassas the same as Prince William County?
faqs.a: No. Manassas is its own independent city, though it is the county seat of Prince William County. The two are separate governments.

faqs.q: When are Manassas real estate taxes due?
faqs.a: Taxes are due December 5 and June 5, and the fiscal year starts July 1.
The Commissioner of the Revenue assesses real property, and the Treasurer collects the tax.

faqs.q: I have an escrow account. Who pays my Manassas tax bill?
faqs.a: Your mortgage company usually pays it. Forward any bill you receive to your lender, since the Treasurer does not send homeowners copies.

faqs.q: Do I pay a transfer tax when I sell a Manassas house?
faqs.a: Virginia charges a grantor tax of 50 cents per $500 of value, and the seller pays it unless the contract says otherwise. See Virginia Code 58.1-802.
